newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-ROOKIE STEWART CINK GETS FIRST PGA TOUR VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ROOKIE STEWART CINK GETS FIRST PGA TOUR VICTORY.

text.p: Rookie Stewart Cink earned his first PGA Tour victory at the $1.5 million Greater Hartford Open, and with a final-round 66 Sunday equalled Greg Norman's 1995 tournament scoring record of 267, 13 under par.

Cink finished a stroke ahead of three golfers: third-round leader Jeff Maggert, who elected not to play it safe on his final hole and paid the price with a bogey to record a one-over-par 71, as well as Brandel Chamblee (66) and Tom Byrum (69).
"I'll never forget this day, to be on top of one of these fields -- to win -- wow, that's really something," said Cink, who at age 24 continues the recent trend of young winners on the PGA Tour.

A star college golfer and the 1996 Nike Tour player of the year with three wins and a single-season earnings record on that cicuit, Cink began the 1997 PGA Tour season with the expectations of many that he would succeed Tiger Woods as rookie of the year.
But Cink got off to a slow start this year, and had his best finish last month with a tie for sixth at Westchester.

"When I got out of school my goal was to play well enough to have a place to play, so I was happy to be on the Nike Tour. I played a lot against Justin (Leonard, the British Open champion) in college, and seeing him win, the different ways he has won out here, made me think about winning," said Cink.

Cink began the final round three strokes behind Maggert, but tied him for the lead with a 35-foot chip-in for birdie on the 10th hole. It would be his last birdie of the round, but pars were enough to ensure the win.

His putting the weakest part of a solid game, Cink missed two birdie chances from inside eight feet on 13 and 15. He got into trouble only on the 17th hole, when his tee shot went into the deep rough on the spectators' hillside.
Without a tournament on the line, Cink might have laid up, but instead he hit a nine-iron over the lake and barely onto the green, two-putting for his par.
Maggert, who hadn't missed a fairway on Saturday, was far less precise off the tee on Sunday. His drive on 15 found the water, but he was able to salvage par.
On the 18th hole, with Cink already in, Maggert's drive left him in deep rough and on a hillside.

Needing birdie to win and a par to force a playoff, Maggert chose not to take the safer route in laying up in front of the lake on the par four, but his second shot skipped over the green and his chip went 40 feet past the pin.
He hit a fine lag putt, but all that earned him was yet another second-place finish, the seventh of his career.

Although the title was his goal, Maggert also needed the Ryder Cup points a win would have brought him. The 80 he earned on Sunday pushed him up from 12th to 11th on the points list, still outside the top 10 automatic selections.

Cink and Maggert were the only two to hold the lead on Sunday, but both Chamblee and Byrum had good chances, and both lipped out birdie putts on the 18th that would have sent the tournament to sudden-death.

Chamblee had the day's most dramatic shot, holing a 90-yard sand wedge for eagle on the 13th hole. He posted his second second-place finish in the last three weeks, having been runner-up previously at Quad Cities.

For Byrum, the 20-footer which burned the hole on 18 was his fifth lip-out of the day. "The putts kept lipping out, and I was thinking, what do I have to do? I was proud of myself for handling the pressure. I'm not disappointed, but I still wish I had tied him," said Byrum.

Cink's victory was worth $270,000 and gave him season earnings of $496,878. The only tour rookie to win this year, Cink is also the first player to follow a season as Nike Tour player of the year with a win on the regular tour.
